newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Lesotho police mutiny seen threatening government.
newsitem.headline: Lesotho police mutiny seen threatening government.

text.p: A Lesotho police mutiny which has led to a nationwide police strike threatens the government of the Southern African mountain kingdom, diplomats there said on Friday.

A Western diplomat in the capital Maseru said:"This government is in crisis and there could be a coup at any time. We are in touch with the government, the king (Letsie III) and all the people who matter."

Eight officers of the Royal Lesotho Mounted Police, resisting arrest for the alleged killing of three fellow officers in 1995, took control of the country's police headquarters in Maseru last Thursday and dismissed the police commissioner. They have been joined by up to 60 other officers.

"The headquarters are occupied by a rebel group of 60 to 70 officers who are fairly well armed and the main core of the group has said they will not give up without a fight... We are in for an interesting time," the diplomat told Reuters by telephone
He said church groups, non-governmental organisations and politicians were mediating with the rebels, but "nobody holds much hope for that."

A meeting of Lesotho's senior police officers on Monday resolved to set up a committee to negotiate an end to the dispute. But the rebels called a nationwide strike of Lesotho's 2,000 police officers from Thursday and diplomats said no police were to be seen on the streets.
Despite the police crisis there was no tension in Maseru, diplomats said.
They said although the army had been instructed to intervene nothing had been done.
"The army has decided to have nothing to do with the situation and the commander has defied all orders to intervene," one said.
The mutineering officers are claiming amnesty under Lesotho's Pardons Act, which stipulates that security force members may not be charged for any crimes committed from 1993 to 1995.

The latest problems in Lesotho are nothing new. For well over a decade the landlocked kingdom, which has a population of nearly two million and is roughly the size of Belgium, has seen military coups and political upheavals.
Most of Lesotho's trade is with South Africa and it belongs to a customs union with South Africa, Botswana and Swaziland.
The country is heavily dependent on remittances from miners working in South Africa. Customs receipts make up about half of government revenue.

"Lesotho is emerging from decades of autocratic rule and with this emerging democracy people are unsure of the roles and responsibilities they have, I suppose you could call this teething troubles," the Western diplomat said.

Problems were exacerbated by a split in the ruling Basotho Congress Party, divided between pragmatists who seek closer economic and political links with South Africa and the region, and those who are more conservative.

Southern African leaders have dismissed joint intervention in the Lesotho crisis. South African President Nelson Mandela has said he is prepared to offer advice to help the kingdom resolve its problems.
